title: A guaranteed tenth reward
prompt: A reward system gives an item independently with probability 0.05 on each of the first nine attempts. If the item has not appeared, it is guaranteed on attempt 10. Let T be the attempt on which the item first appears. What is P(T = 10)?
recognize: The final success is guaranteed, so this is a capped first-success process.
T = 10 means every one of the first nine attempts failed.

steps.title: Find the failure chance
steps.why: A trial either gives the item or does not. The failure chance is the complement of 0.05.

steps.title: Describe reaching attempt 10
steps.why: A previous success would stop the process. Exactly nine failures are needed to reach the guaranteed attempt.

steps.title: Multiply the independent failures
steps.why: Independent events multiply; attempt 10 contributes a factor of 1 because success is guaranteed.

pitfalls: Do not multiply by 0.05 on attempt 10.
There are nine failures, not ten.

title: Condition on a staircase CDF
prompt: The CDF is F(x) = 0 for x < 0; 0.12 for 0 ≤ x < 1; 0.40 for 1 ≤ x < 2; 0.76 for 2 ≤ x < 3; 1 for x ≥ 3. What is P(1 ≤ X ≤ 2 | X > 0)?
recognize: The CDF gives cumulative masses, so subtract to isolate an interval.
The word given or the vertical bar means divide by the probability of the given event.

steps.title: Identify numerator and denominator
steps.why: The event 1 ≤ X ≤ 2 already lies inside X > 0, so their intersection is the same interval.

steps.title: Include both endpoint masses
steps.why: The support is {0,1,2,3}. To include 1, subtract the CDF at 0, which removes only values below 1.

steps.title: Find the given event
steps.why: X > 0 excludes exactly the mass at 0.

steps.title: Normalize within the given event
steps.why: Among the probability mass remaining above 0, 0.64 is in the desired interval.

pitfalls: Subtracting F(1) would wrongly exclude X = 1.
The denominator is 0.88, not 1.

title: Normalize a linear PMF
prompt: P(X = x) = c(2x + 1) for x ∈ {0,1,2,3,4}, and is 0 otherwise. What is P(X ≥ 3)?
recognize: An unknown PMF constant c requires total mass 1.
X ≥ 3 retains only x = 3 and x = 4 from this support.

steps.title: Normalize the PMF
steps.why: Every possible value must be included when finding c.

steps.title: Solve for the multiplier
steps.why: The unscaled weights add to 25, so each weight is divided by 25.

steps.title: Add the requested masses
steps.why: Only 3 and 4 satisfy the inclusive inequality.

answerText: 0.64, the combined probability of X = 3 or X = 4.
pitfalls: Do not use c = 1/5: the five values have unequal weights.

title: Eight failed reconnect attempts

title: Which model is not binomial?

title: Delivery rating: find the missing mass

title: Waiting beyond twenty test runs
prompt: Each run of an automated test suite independently detects a hidden bug with probability 0.08, constant from run to run. steps.why: The unconditional range divided by four-failure probability gives the same answer.

refs.label: Evaluate and cross-check with a ratio

pitfalls: Do not reset 6 through 8 to future positions 1 through 3.
Attempt 5 must fail for first success to be at least 6.

refs.label: Evaluate and cross-check with a ratio

title: Ninety-minute requests given at least one
prompt: Requests follow a Poisson process at rate 1.9 per hour. During 90 minutes, given that at least one request occurs, what is the probability that between two and four requests occur, inclusive? Round to three decimal places. For Z ~ Pois(λ), P(Z = k) = e^(−λ)λᵏ/k!.
recognize: The requested window is 1.5 hours, so λ differs from the hourly rate.
Given at least one requires dividing by the positive-count probability.

steps.title: Scale to the 90-minute interval
steps.why: Convert the duration to the units of the given rate.

steps.title: Sum the desired counts
steps.why: The numerator includes 2,3,4, all of which already satisfy the condition.

steps.title: Find the given-event mass
steps.why: At least one excludes only zero.

steps.title: Normalize and round
steps.why: Divide the requested positive counts by all positive-count mass.

pitfalls: Using λ = 1.9 describes one hour, not ninety minutes.
Do not omit the denominator just because the numerator already has positive counts.

title: A binomial middle range given at least two
prompt: Let X ~ Bin(12,0.37). Find P(2 ≤ X ≤ 4 | X ≥ 2), to three decimal places.
recognize: The model is given; first identify the numerator range and the given-event denominator.
The denominator X ≥ 2 has a short complement at counts 0 and 1.

steps.title: Set up the conditional ratio
steps.why: The target 2 through 4 is wholly inside the given event of at least 2.

steps.title: Evaluate the range
steps.why: Sum exactly the three binomial masses at 2,3,4.

steps.title: Evaluate the denominator by complement
steps.why: Remove counts 0 and 1 from total mass 1.

steps.title: Divide and round
steps.why: The quotient is the proportion of at-least-two cases that have no more than four successes.

pitfalls: P(X ≥ 2) is not the same denominator as P(X ≤ 4).

title: High-severity support tickets
prompt: A randomly selected support ticket has severity X ∈ {0,1,2,3} with respective probabilities 0.45,0.30,0.20,0.05. What is P(X ≥ 2)?
recognize: A finite PMF table lets you select the allowed values directly.
The inclusive inequality X ≥ 2 retains 2 and 3.

steps.title: Check the PMF
steps.why: The masses are nonnegative and add to 1.

steps.title: Select the support values
steps.why: The high-severity event is the union of X = 2 and X = 3.

steps.title: Add the disjoint masses
steps.why: A ticket cannot have both scores, so these probabilities add.

answerText: 0.25: a 25% chance that severity is at least 2.
pitfalls: Adding all masses through 2 gives P(X ≤ 2), which is a different event.

title: Three tasks from one missing PMF
prompt: Y takes values 0,1,2,3 with PMF masses 0.18,c,2c,0.22. Which triple gives c, P(Y ≥ 2), and P(Y is even), respectively?
recognize: Normalize c using the entire table, then handle each requested event separately.
Zero is an even integer and must be included in the even event.

steps.title: Normalize the PMF
steps.why: The four probability masses exhaust all possibilities.

steps.title: Select values at least 2
steps.why: The event includes values 2 and 3.

steps.title: Select the even values
steps.why: The even support values are 0 and 2.

pitfalls: Do not forget that 0 is even.
Use c = 0.20 for both entries c and 2c.

title: Read a point, interval, and tail from a CDF
prompt: An integer-valued X has F(0)=0.15, F(1)=0.50, F(2)=0.85, and F(3)=1. Which triple gives P(X = 2), P(0 < X ≤ 2), and P(X ≥ 2), respectively?
recognize: A point probability is a CDF jump.
An inclusive lower tail endpoint requires excluding only values below it.

steps.title: Find the mass at 2
steps.why: Since X is integer-valued, values strictly below 2 are at most 1.

steps.title: Find the interval with strict lower endpoint
steps.why: Subtracting F(0) removes all values through 0, leaving just 0 < X ≤ 2.

refs.label: Find the interval with strict lower endpoint

steps.title: Find the inclusive upper tail
steps.why: To include X = 2, subtract only values at most 1.

pitfalls: 1 − F(2) would find X > 2, not X ≥ 2.

refs.label: Find the interval with strict lower endpoint

title: One feature-flag response
prompt: A feature flag is shown to one randomly selected user. X = 1 if the user enables it, and X = 0 otherwise. P(X = 1) = 0.35. Which states the distribution and remaining PMF value correctly?
recognize: One binary response coded 0 or 1 is Bernoulli.
The parameter is the probability of the value coded 1.

steps.title: Identify the single binary trial
steps.why: Only one user response is recorded; there is no waiting time or multi-trial count.

steps.title: Read the success parameter
steps.why: Enabling the feature is the event coded 1.

steps.title: Use the complementary mass
steps.why: The two mutually exclusive outcomes exhaust the experiment.

pitfalls: The success label refers to X = 1; it does not imply that outcome is desirable.

title: At least six critical hits out of eight
prompt: In a game, each of eight attacks independently produces a critical hit with probability 0.60. X is the number of critical hits. Find P(X ≥ 6).
recognize: Eight fixed independent attacks with constant p = 0.60 give a binomial count.
Only counts 6,7,8 satisfy the requested event, so a direct short sum is convenient.

steps.title: Choose the model
steps.why: There are fixed n = 8 binary trials with independence and common success chance.

steps.title: List the included counts
steps.why: At least six critical hits means 6, 7, or 8.

steps.title: Write each binomial term
steps.why: For each count, choose the successful attack positions and multiply successes and failures.

steps.title: Add and interpret
steps.why: The three possible counts are disjoint, so their probabilities add.

answerText: 0.31539456, about a 31.5% chance of at least six critical hits.
pitfalls: P(X = 6) alone does not include seven or eight hits.

title: API succeeds by attempt five after three failures
prompt: An API request succeeds with probability 0.25 on each independent attempt. X is the number of attempts until first success. Given that the first three attempts failed, what is the probability of success by attempt five?
recognize: The three failures are known; attempts 4 and 5 are the two remaining opportunities.
Constant p makes the future wait memoryless.

steps.title: Count the remaining opportunities
steps.why: By attempt five leaves only attempts 4 and 5 after three completed failures.

steps.title: Use memorylessness
steps.why: Conditioning on the past failures does not alter the independent future attempts.

steps.title: Take the complement of two failures
steps.why: Both remaining attempts fail with probability 0.75².

refs.label: Take the complement of two failures

pitfalls: 1 − 0.75⁵ ignores the known failures and counts five future opportunities.

refs.label: Take the complement of two failures

title: No server alerts over two hours
prompt: A server receives an average of 2.5 critical alerts per hour under a Poisson model. What is the probability of no alerts during a two-hour period?
recognize: The count window is twice the one-hour rate interval.
No alerts is a Poisson zero-count event.

steps.title: Scale the rate
steps.why: A two-hour window has twice the expected count under the same constant rate.

steps.title: Evaluate the PMF at zero
steps.why: At k = 0, the power and factorial factors equal 1.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.why: With a mean of five alerts, a zero-alert interval is possible but uncommon.
steps.math: e⁻⁵ ≈ 0.006738 → about a 0.674% chance of no alerts in two hours

pitfalls: Do not double a probability: double λ, then evaluate the new PMF.
